description.en: Learn how convolutional filters slide over an image to detect edges, textures, and features via kernel operations.

story_variants.en:
## Convolutions: Filters That See

A **convolution** slides a small grid (called a **kernel** or **filter**) over the input image. At each position, it computes a dot product between the kernel and the patch of pixels — producing a **feature map**.

### How It Works

```
Input patch:  [[1, 2, 3],    Kernel: [[-1, 0, 1],
               [4, 5, 6],            [-2, 0, 2],
               [7, 8, 9]]            [-1, 0, 1]]

Convolution: (1×-1)+(2×0)+(3×1)+(4×-2)+(5×0)+(6×2)+(7×-1)+(8×0)+(9×1)
           = -1+0+3-8+0+12-7+0+9 = 8
```

### Key Terminology

| Term | Meaning |
|------|---------|
| Kernel / Filter | Small weight matrix (e.g. 3×3) |
| Stride | How many pixels to skip each step |
| Padding | Zero-rows/cols added to border |
| Feature Map | Output of applying a filter |
| Depth | Number of filters applied |

### Output Size Formula

```
output_size = (input_size − kernel_size + 2×padding) / stride + 1
```

Example: 28×28 input, 3×3 kernel, stride=1, padding=0 → 26×26 output.

### What Filters Learn

```python
import numpy as np

def convolve2d(image, kernel):
    kh, kw = kernel.shape
    oh = image.shape[0] - kh + 1
    ow = image.shape[1] - kw + 1
    output = np.zeros((oh, ow))
    for i in range(oh):
        for j in range(ow):
            output[i, j] = np.sum(image[i:i+kh, j:j+kw] * kernel)
    return output
```

> **Key Concept:** The same filter is applied to every position (weight sharing). This gives CNNs **translation invariance** — a cat is a cat whether it's on the left or right of the image.

explanation.en: Sobel edge-detection kernel for vertical edges

output: Weight sharing: same kernel scanned entire image

import torch
import torch.nn as nn

conv = nn.Conv2d(in_channels=1, out_channels=8, kernel_size=3, padding=1)
input_img = torch.randn(1, 1, 28, 28)
output = conv(input_img)
print(f'Input:  {input_img.shape}')
print(f'Output: {output.shape}')
print(f'Kernel shape: {conv.weight.shape}')
print(f'Parameters: {conv.weight.numel() + conv.bias.numel()}')

q.en: Why can a CNN recognise a cat whether it is on the left or the right of an image?

en: The same filter is applied at every position (weight sharing)
A large stride skips over the empty parts of the image
Padding adds zeros so the cat is always centred
Each pixel position has its own separate filter

பெரிய stride படத்தின் காலியான பகுதிகளைத் தாண்டிவிடுகிறது
Padding பூஜ்யங்களைச் சேர்ப்பதால் பூனை எப்போதும் நடுவில் இருக்கும்
ஒவ்வொரு pixel நிலைக்கும் தனி filter உள்ளது

en: Nothing changes; NumPy adjusts the size automatically
Output has one extra row filled with garbage values
It raises an IndexError when slicing the image
Output has one row too few; the last valid position is skipped

under_the_hood.summary: A convolution slides a small grid of weights over the image, multiplies it element-wise with the patch underneath and adds the products into one number per position; the same weights are reused at every position, so each filter becomes a detector for one pattern.

steps.title: One position: multiply and add
steps.body: Patch [[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6], [7, 8, 9]] with kernel [[-1, 0, 1], [-2, 0, 2], [-1, 0, 1]] gives -1 + 0 + 3 - 8 + 0 + 12 - 7 + 0 + 9 = 8. That single number goes into the output map at this position. Deep learning libraries actually compute cross-correlation (no kernel flip), but call it convolution.

steps.title: Slide to build a feature map
steps.body: Move the kernel one pixel (stride 1) and repeat. On a 28 x 28 image a 3 x 3 kernel fits in 26 x 26 positions: output = (input - kernel + 2 x padding) / stride + 1. With padding 1 the output stays 28 x 28; with stride 2 it is (28 - 3 + 2) / 2 + 1, rounded down to 14.

steps.title: The kernel is a pattern detector
steps.body: This kernel responds to left-to-right brightness changes. On a patch with a vertical edge, columns 0, 0, 10, it gives 10 + 20 + 10 = 40. On a flat patch where every pixel is 5 it gives 0. High output means 'my pattern is here'. In a CNN these weights are not designed by hand; training learns them.

steps.title: Channels and filter banks
steps.body: A colour image has 3 channels, so each kernel is 3 x 3 x 3 and sums across all channels into one output map. A layer with 16 such filters makes 16 maps and has 3 x 3 x 3 x 16 + 16 biases = 448 parameters, whatever the image size, because the same weights are shared across positions.

steps.title: Stacking widens the view
steps.body: One 3 x 3 layer sees 3 x 3 pixels; a second layer on top sees 5 x 5 of the original image, a third 7 x 7. Early layers learn edges and colours, later ones combine them into textures, parts and objects. Weight sharing also means a feature is detected wherever it appears in the image.

under_the_hood.takeaway: A convolution is a small dot product repeated at every position with shared weights. That gives far fewer parameters than dense layers, detection anywhere in the image, and, when stacked, a growing field of view.
